notes: Help example: aov(log(P / (100 - P)) ~ Species / Isolate + Error(Rep / Tray)) with P = 100 * (Resistant + 1) / (Seedlings + 2), an empirical logit of the resistant share of each tray's seedlings, written in the columns. The Error strata translate to lmer as a Rep random intercept (as gomez.splitplot.subsample); Tray, 13 per replicate run with one row each, is the residual stratum and goes to ignore. Rep has three runs, kept since the source fits it as a stratum. The fit is Gaussian on the transformed share, hence family gaussian on a binomial response with Seedlings as trials. Isolate codes repeat across the two species (Species / Isolate), so the nested term is Species:Isolate; TypeA and TypeB recode Isolate per species. Source Welham et al. (2015) Statistical Methods in Biology; smbdata has no vignette and its data-raw holds only the book's .DAT files.

Help example: aov(Grain ~ Irrigation * Species + Error(Block/WholePlot/Subplot)), a split plot with irrigation on the whole plots and weed species on the subplots of four blocks. Translated to lmer as Block and Block:WholePlot random intercepts (WholePlot is coded 1-2 within each block in the package's data-raw/original/COMPETITION.DAT); Subplot, one row each, is the residual stratum. Four blocks, kept since the source fits them as a stratum. Source Welham et al. (2015).

Help example: anova(lm(Yield ~ Block + Size * Type)), a randomized complete block design of five blocks of five plots of willow cuttings, not every type-by-size combination present. Block is fitted fixed and rendered as a random intercept (mead.germination ruling). Its five levels meet the five-level rule, but no source establishes that they are sampled from a larger population. Plot, one row each within a block, is the residual unit. Source Welham et al. (2015).

Help example: summary(aov(Yield ~ factor(N) + Error(Block/Plot))), a randomized complete block of three blocks x four nitrogen rates (Rothamsted, 1996). Translated to lmer as a Block random intercept; Plot, one row each, is the residual stratum. N enters as a factor, so types declares it categorical. Three blocks, kept since the source fits them as a stratum. Source Welham et al. (2015).

Help example: aov(sqrt(Fwt) ~ Herbicide * Population + Error(Rep/DPot)), a randomized complete block of five replicates of 27 pots (three herbicides x nine black-grass populations). Translated to lmer as a Rep random intercept; DPot, one row each, is the residual stratum. Type groups the herbicides by chemical group (A and C against B), a recode of Herbicide, so it is ignored. Source Welham et al. (2015), data from R. Hull, Rothamsted.

formula: log((Infected + 1) / (Live - Infected + 1)) ~ Host * factor(Cadaver) * Ladybird + (1 | Run)
notes: Help example: summary(aov(log(P / (100 - P)) ~ Host * Cadaver * Ladybird + Error(Run/DPlant))) with P = 100 * (Infected + 1) / (Live + 2) and Cadaver = factor(Cadaver), an empirical logit of the infected share of the live aphids, written in the columns. The fit is Gaussian on the transformed share, hence family gaussian on a binomial response with Live as trials. Translated to lmer as a Run random intercept; DPlant (36 per run, one row each) is the residual stratum. Run has two levels, kept since the source fits it as a stratum. Source Welham et al. (2015).

Help example: aov(OilYield ~ Line + Error(Block/Plot)), a randomized complete block of three blocks x 14 lupin breeding lines. Translated to lmer as a Block random intercept; Plot, one row each, is the residual stratum. NPlant (plants per square metre) is another of the trial's assessed traits that the model leaves out, ignored as an alternate variate. Three blocks, kept since the source fits them as a stratum. Source Welham et al. (2015).

Help example: summary(aov(RowYield ~ Fungicide + Error(Block/Plot/Row))), the row yields within the plots of a randomized complete block of four blocks x five plots. Translated to lmer as Block and Block:Plot random intercepts (Plot is coded 1-5 within each block); Row, one row each, is the residual stratum. Four blocks, kept since the source fits them as a stratum. smbdata's potato holds the plot means of these rows. Source Welham et al. (2015).

formula: cbind(Eaten, Total - Eaten) ~ Sex * Prey + (1 | Row)
notes: Help example: glm(cbind(Eaten, Total) ~ Row + Sex * Prey, family = binomial()), a randomized complete block of 15 rows (blocks that combine occasions and spatial replicates) x four dishes. The description calls Eaten binomial out of the six prey offered (Total), so cbind(Eaten, Total) is an evident slip for cbind(Eaten, Total - Eaten) and the intended model is filed (voorspoels ruling). Row is fitted fixed and rendered as a random intercept (mead.germination ruling); its 15 levels meet the five-level rule, though no source establishes their sampling. Dish, one row each within a row, is the residual unit. Source Welham et al. (2015).

Help example: summary(aov(log10(Weeds) ~ Year * Treatment + Error(Farm/Field/DHalf))) with Year = factor(Year): the Farm Scale Evaluations of GM herbicide-tolerant spring oilseed rape, each field split into a conventional and a GM half. Translated to lmer as Farm and Farm:Field random intercepts (Field is coded 1-3 within each farm); DHalf, one row each, is the residual stratum. A Gaussian fit to log10 counts, hence family gaussian on a count. Seedbank, the baseline the description says the analysis controls for, is not in the example and stays a usable column. Source Welham et al. (2015).

RESPONSE INFERRED: nine morphometric measurements on 104 mountain brushtail possums trapped at seven sites (Lindenmayer et al. 1995). The page and the book's code (Maindonald, Braun and Andrews 2024, jhmaindonald.github.io/Rcode, subsection 1.2.1 and chapter 9) only plot, bootstrap a correlation, run principal components and a linear discriminant analysis of site, and fit no model. Possums repeat within trapping site, so site groups the rows (a cluster the source treats as independent, as ROS). Total length is the measurement subsection 1.2.1 compares by sex and Pop (bwplot(Pop ~ totlngth | sex)); Pop classifies the sites (Victoria against the rest) and is a site-level covariate. The other eight measurements are alternate responses; age is a usable column. RULE GAP: site is also the class the discriminant analysis predicts (crabs and iris were excluded as discrimination tables), but here it indexes the sampling cluster.

Help example: lm(log(Time) ~ log(Distance)), the progression of men's track world records from 1912. Each race (100m, mile, ...) contributes its successive records, so race groups the rows and is rendered as a random intercept beside log(Distance), which is constant within a race. year is a usable column. RULE GAP: the races are the standard event distances rather than a sample, and each race's records form a short series; the five-level rule and the flat-table definition (a column indexing a unit the rows repeat within) point different ways.

Help example and Maindonald and Braun (2010, section 10.2; Maindonald, Braun and Andrews 2024, section 7.3): science.lmer <- lmer(like ~ sex + PrivPub + (1 | school) + (1 | school:class), na.action = na.exclude). class is coded within school, so the class term is school:class; Class names the same classes as one factor and is ignored as its alias. The book's preferred science1.lmer drops the school term, whose component is negligible, a variant with one level fewer (SASmixed ruling). like is a 1-12 score of more than ten values, so continuous. State is a usable column.

formula: ct ~ Cultivar + Dose + factor(year) + (-1 + Dose | gp)
notes: Exercise 7.6 code of Maindonald, Braun and Andrews (2024, jhmaindonald.github.io/Rcode, chapter 7) and the end of the 3rd edition's chapter 10 script (maths-people.anu.edu.au/~johnm/r-book/3edn/scripts/mlm.html): cult.lmer <- lmer(ct ~ Cultivar + Dose + factor(year) + (-1 + Dose | gp), data = sorption, REML = TRUE). gp is one replicate batch of apples of a cultivar, its rows the injected doses, with a Dose slope per gp and no gp intercept in the source. The second fit, cultdose.lmer (Cultivar/Dose, a dose slope per cultivar), has the same response and grouping. ct, the concentration-time product of methyl bromide, is the response; the readings m5 to m120 it is computed over are ignored, and rep, year.rep and inyear index replicates and doses.

The page lists the St. Vincent corn fertilizer trials of Andrews and Herzberg (1985, pp. 339-353): plots in four blocks (I-IV, coded within site) at each site, with 12 treatments coded by three digits for the fertilizer levels, and fits no model. Rendered with treatment fixed and site and site:block random intercepts, the structure Maindonald and Braun (2010, section 10.1; 2024, section 7.1) fit to the Antiguan counterpart ant111b (lmer(harvwt ~ 1 + (1 | site))). plot, one row each within a block, is the residual unit; id, code and island are identifiers. vince111b holds the block averages of treatment 111.

Maindonald and Braun (2010, section 10.4; Maindonald, Braun and Andrews 2024, section 7.5): it2.lmer <- lmer(log(it) ~ (tint + target + agegp + sex)^2 + (1 | id)), the model the anova of it1 (main effects), it2 (all two-factor interactions) and it3 (all interactions) selects, refitted by REML for the estimates. Each of the 26 subjects (id) saw three tint levels and two target contrasts (Burns et al. 1999). csoa, the second visual-performance time, is only plotted, so it is ignored as an alternate response. case repeats id; age is a usable column that agegp groups.

Help pages JoSAE-package and eblup.mse.f.wrap, and the JoSAE vignette: lme(biomass.ha ~ mean.canopy.ht, data = JoSAE.sample.data, random = ~1 | domain.ID), the unit-level EBLUP model of Breidenbach and Astrup (2012): Norwegian National Forest Inventory plots in small-area domains, above-ground biomass on photogrammetric mean canopy height. sae.ul.f refits the same model. sample.ID is the plot identifier.

JoSAE vignette (inst/doc/JoSAE.R, chunks 10-11): lme(HACorn ~ PixelsCorn + PixelsSoybeans, random = ~1 | domain.ID) on landsat[-33, ], domain.ID a numeric code of CountyName, so the fit leaves out the segment the outlier column flags (Battese et al. 1988, p. 28). The error-components model of Battese, Harter and Fuller (1988): sample segments in 12 Iowa counties, survey hectares of corn on LANDSAT pixel counts. SegementID numbers the segments within a county; SegmentsInCounty and the county mean pixel counts are population values for the EBLUP, not fitted; HASoybeans is the second response (row 2).

Second response of the same segments: Battese, Harter and Fuller (1988, JASA 83: 28-36), the page's reference, fit soybean hectares on both pixel counts with a county random intercept, as for corn (row 1); recalled from the paper, as the hand sample recorded it for rabe_hesketh cropareas.dta. The JoSAE vignette fits corn only, without segment 33.

Help pages sae.ul.f and sae.al.f: sae.ul.f(samp.data = ulal.sub.samp.dat, formula = w.VMPRHA ~ elev.mean + elev.mean.sq, domain.col = 'stand.ID', k.ij = k.ij.one), the unit-level EBLUP that sae.ul.f fits by nlme's lme with a stand random intercept (Breidenbach et al. 2018): 73 sample plots in 15 forest stands, timber volume per hectare on photogrammetric mean height and its square. The second example sets k.ij = k.ij.em.0.48, a fixed variance weight for heteroscedasticity, with the same response and grouping; both k.ij columns are weights and are ignored. elev.mean.sq is stored in the table and named as the source's formula names it. The area-level example fits stand means built from this table and ulal.sub.dom.dat.
